title: Changing an object through a parameter
goal: Pass addresses of the caller’s objects and save the first value before swapping them.

prerequisites.text: You need function arguments and parameters, plus reading and writing through a dereference.

terms.title: Pointer parameter
terms.definition: A local copy of the passed address. A write through that address may update the passed object.

terms.title: Temporary copy
terms.definition: A separate object that preserves an old value before it is overwritten.

terms.title: Alias
terms.definition: Another expression naming the same object. Equal pointers that are valid for access can dereference to one object.

sections.title: Swap the caller’s objects
paragraphs: A function must order two measurement limits. Pass the addresses of the existing objects, so the results go into the caller’s variables.
C passes each argument by value. Here the copied value is an address, so a and &low point to the same low object. Changing the parameter a itself would change only its local copy of the address.
Establish pointer validity before reading or writing. In the example the addresses come from two live int objects, and the function also rejects NULL.

sections.title: Swap 9 and 4
paragraphs: Save the first value separately, then trace the assignments in their execution order.
steps: The swap call passes the addresses of low and high. The check accepts both live objects.
saved = *a preserves 9 in a separate object. *a = *b changes low to 4.
*b = saved writes the earlier value 9 to high.

sections.title: Save the integer before overwriting
paragraphs: In swap(&low, high), the second argument supplies an integer. Clang rejects it for an int * parameter. Use &high to get the second object’s address.
The declaration int *saved = a makes another pointer to the same object. After *a = *b, a read through *saved sees the new value. Copy the old integer into a separate int before writing.

sections.title: One address can be passed twice
paragraphs: Predict normalize(&low, &low) when low is 6. Both reads give 6, so the already-ordered branch returns without writing. The contract allows this pair.

reading.author: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14
reading.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 — Programming languages — C
reading.purpose: Check passing arguments by value, dereferencing and assignment.

selfcheck.prompt: After *a = *b in the example with 9 and 4, what are low and saved?
feedback: The separate integer preserved 9 before the write to low.
The high value 4 is copied into low.
The separate integer saved still holds the old value.

selfcheck.prompt: What does normalize(&low, &low) return when low is 6?
feedback: Both parameters read the same value 6.
The first read does not exceed the second, so there is no write.
Both pointers can refer to the same live object.

selfcheck.prompt: The starter declares saved as int * and assigns it low. Trace the two writes for input 12 and -2. How can you keep 12 before the first write?
selfcheck.feedback: After *low = *high both objects hold -2. *saved reads -2 too because it points to low. Copy *low into a separate int before the first write.

practice.title: Order two limits
practice.task: Read two integers from -99 to 99 on separate lines, a lower and an upper limit. The normalize function takes addresses of two live int objects, checks for NULL and swaps values only when they are out of order. Return 1 for a swap, 0 for an already ordered pair and -1 for NULL without writing. Print both values and the swap indicator separated by spaces. Print invalid for malformed input. Ignore subsequent lines.
practice.hint: Decide whether saved should hold the address low or the integer stored there before the assignment.
criteria: 12 and -2 give -2 12 1. -2 and 12 give -2 12 0. 3 and 3 give 3 3 0.
The NULL checks precede every dereference.
If valid addresses are equal, the value stays the same and the return is 0.

steps.action: Open Practice with input 12 and -2. Select Run my code.
steps.why: Trace what the saved pointer reads after the write to low.
steps.expected: The starter prints -2 -2 1. The expected result is -2 12 1.

steps.action: Save a copy of the first integer instead of another address, then rerun.
steps.why: An independent integer retains the original value.

steps.action: Run -2 and 12, then 3 and 3, in separate runs.
steps.why: Check both the ordered and equal cases.

exercises.title: Independent transfer
exercises.task: Save a copy of your corrected main.c in a separate text file. In the editor, replace the second argument of normalize with &low for one run. With input 8 and 2, explain both numbers and the returned indicator. Restore your saved code.
criteria: Output 8 2 0 shows that comparing 8 with itself is already ordered.
With the distinct addresses restored, the same input gives 2 8 1.

teaching.scene: Two thermostat limits are reversed. Trace the swap so the original first number is still available after the first write.

predict.prompt: Before swap, low and high are 9 and 4. What does each object hold immediately after *a = *b? What does saved hold at that point?
predict.answer: Both objects temporarily hold 4. saved preserved 9 before the write to low. The last assignment takes 9 from saved and writes it to high.

apply.prompt: With low = 8 and high = 2, reason through normalize(&low, &low). Does it swap, and what triple does the same main print?
apply.answer: It compares 8 with itself and returns from the already-ordered branch without writing. The output is 8 2 0.

practice.strategy: Check both pointers and decide whether a swap is necessary before writing. Save the earlier integer before the first assignment. Check reversed, ordered and equal pairs.
practice.diagnosis: With 12 and -2, the starter prints -2 -2 1. The second value is lost because saved contains the address of the object that was already changed. Compare the temporary's type with that of the value being saved.

syntax.explanation: A separate int preserves the earlier value. A pointer parameter receives a copy of the address, so access through it reaches the caller's object.
syntax.mistake: int *saved = first creates another path to the same object. After a write through first, a read through saved sees the updated value.
